APPLE’S SILENT KILLER: The Invisible Disease Threatening the World’s Most Valuable Company 💀 | Steve Jobs Philosophy vs Tim Cook

Apple — the world’s most admired tech company — is facing a deadly invisible disease.

A silent killer that looks harmless from the outside… but destroys giants from within.

It’s the same disease that killed Nokia, Blackberry, and Kodak.
👉 What exactly is this “disease”?
👉 Why did it infect Apple — the $3.8 Trillion giant?
👉 Can Apple survive it, or is the fall already beginning?
👉 And what can every entrepreneur learn from Steve Jobs’s missing philosophy?

This video breaks down the truth behind Apple’s decline in innovation, the rise of profit mindset under Tim Cook, and how The Innovator’s Dilemma is silently eating Apple from the inside.

🍏 APPLE’S CURRENT STATUS

Apple is still the 3rd most valuable company in the world with a market cap of $3.8 trillion.

It makes $130 billion profit every year, and its brand value is unmatched.

People still stand in line for iPhones.

Everything looks perfect on the surface — but that’s what makes it dangerous.

Because the disease Apple is facing is a “Silent Killer.”

💡 THE ROOT CAUSE: DEPENDENCE ON STEVE JOBS’ LEGACY

In 2024, Apple made $391 billion in total revenue.

But over 90% of it still comes from products created under Steve Jobs —iPhone, Mac, iPad, and Apple’s core software services.

Tim Cook became CEO in 2011.

Even after 14 years, only 10% of Apple’s revenue comes from products built under his leadership — like AirPods or Apple Watch.

Both are minor successes, not revolutionary.

Apple once led the world by creating the future.

Now, it’s maintaining it.

🚨 THE DISEASE: THE INNOVATOR’S DILEMMA

This is the same trap that destroyed once-great companies:
 • Depending on old products for safety
 • Avoiding risky innovation
 • Prioritizing profit over philosophy

Tim Cook is a brilliant operations leader.

But Apple has shifted from a Vision-Driven Company to a Business-Driven Company.

It’s no longer “thinking different.”

It’s “thinking safe.”

🔥 THE LOST PHILOSOPHY OF STEVE JOBS

Steve Jobs believed in five timeless principles that made Apple legendary:
 1. Think Different. Challenge rules.
 2. Change the World. Don’t just build — revolutionize.
 3. Empower People with Technology.
 4. Focus & Simplicity. Cut distractions. Perfect one thing.
 5. Stay Hungry. Stay Foolish. Never lose the hunger to innovate.

After his death in 2011, Apple slowly drifted away from these principles.
The Vision Pro headset failed.
The Apple Car project collapsed after wasting 10 years and $10 billion.
And while AI is transforming the world, Apple is outsourcing innovation to OpenAI and Google instead of leading it.

⚠️ THE FUTURE

Apple today behaves more like a financial machine than a creative lab.
It’s optimizing, not imagining.
Improving, not inventing.
Following, not leading.
And that’s why — if it doesn’t reignite Steve Jobs’s mindset —
Apple might soon join the list of great companies that faded, not failed.

Because the moment a company loses its hunger to innovate,
the countdown to its fall begins.

 • The business psychology of “The Innovator’s Dilemma”
 • Why Steve Jobs’s philosophy can still save Apple
 • Lessons every entrepreneur must learn to avoid the same mistake

snippet.title: After Renee Good’s Killing, a Snowball, and Then Tear Gas | FRONTLINE + @ProPublica
snippet.description:
Five days after an ICE agent fatally shot activist Renee Good, @frontline & @ProPublica filmed as tensions ran high in the Minneapolis neighborhood where Good had been killed. A protester threw a snowball. Federal agents responded with tear gas, pepper balls and pepper spray, hitting members of the reporting team in the face. "We see just use of excessive force after use of excess force," said a former DOJ official who looked at the team's footage.

This video is drawn from FRONTLINE and ProPublica's documentary "Caught in the Crackdown," which is available to stream in full:  https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MbPBVFRJQmk

snippet.title: The Company Behind AI, Data Centers & Green Energy | Bhagyanagar India Ltd
snippet.description:
In this episode of the GreenSharks, we sit down with Mr. Devendra Surana — Managing Director of Bhagyanagar India Ltd, a Hyderabad-based copper products manufacturer with a market capitalization of approximately ₹1,000 crore.

Over the last four decades, Bhagyanagar India has built a strong presence across the copper value chain, converting copper scrap into value-added copper products used in power infrastructure, transmission & distribution, telecom, renewable energy, railways, electrical equipment, and industrial applications. As India invests heavily in AI infrastructure, data centers, renewable energy, EVs, and grid modernization, copper continues to remain one of the most critical materials enabling this transformation.

In this conversation, we discuss the company's journey, industry dynamics, copper demand outlook, the role of recycling and value addition, opportunities emerging from India's infrastructure buildout, and Bhagyanagar India's plans for the future.

We believe that the right management can make or break a company's future. As part of our commitment to empowering retail investors, we're inviting you to submit your questions for the promoters of the following companies whom we'll be interviewing next on our Green Sharks Podcast.

snippet.title: Immigration Under President Trump’s First Term | Kids Caught in the Crackdown (full documentary)
snippet.description:
With @AssociatedPress, an Emmy Award-winning examination into conditions inside federally-funded shelter programs for detained migrant children and the lasting impact on kids who were held in U.S. government custody. (Aired 2019)

This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://bit.ly/47DFzCb

And support your local PBS station here: https://www.pbs.org/donate

Detention of migrant children climbed to historic levels during President Donald Trump’s first term. Drawing on confidential government data obtained by @AssociatedPress, "Caught in the Crackdown” revealed how many migrant kids were being held — and where — at any given time.

With unique access — including inside a “tender age” shelter that held some of the youngest children in government custody — the film illuminated what happened when a child apprehended by Customs and Border Protection was handed over to the Department of Health and Human Services, known as HHS. The documentary examined how changes in policies for how sponsors were vetted meant kids were held in government custody for longer and longer periods, and in larger and larger numbers.

In 2020, the documentary was honored with a News Emmy in the “Outstanding Continuing Coverage of a News Story in a Newsmagazine” category. 

“Kids Caught in the Crackdown” was a FRONTLINE production with Five O’Clock Films in partnership with The Associated Press. The writers, producers and directors were Daffodil Altan and Andrés Cediel. The co-producer was Sasha Joelle Achilli. The reporters were Garance Burke and Martha Mendoza. The correspondent was Daffodil Altan. The senior producer was Frank Koughan. The international investigations editor for AP was Ron Nixon. The editor-in-chief and executive producer of FRONTLINE is  Raney Aronson-Rath.

snippet.title: Did India just get hit with an 18.5% US tariff? Not exactly.
snippet.description:
The U.S. Supreme Court blocked emergency tariffs by Donald Trump but Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 was used to impose a 15% global surcharge.

India isn’t being singled out.

3.5% base tariff + 15% surcharge = 18.5% total.

From 50% to 18%, so technically, back to square one.

snippet.title: This Is How India's Most Popular Telecom Company Aircel Disappeared
snippet.description:
This Is How India's Most Popular Telecom Company Aircel Disappeared ! Aman Sharma
There was a time when Aircel was one of India's most popular telecom networks. Founded by C. Sivasankaran in 1999, the company grew rapidly thanks to its strong connectivity and customer service, eventually becoming India's 5th largest telecom operator.

But in 2005, everything changed.

Sivasankaran sold Aircel to Malaysia's Maxis Communications for ₹3,400 crore. Later, he alleged that he was pressured into the deal, triggering the famous Aircel-Maxis case—one of India's longest-running telecom controversies.

While legal battles continued, Aircel spent heavily on expansion and advertising. Then came the 2G spectrum controversy, adding more pressure to the company.

The final blow arrived in 2016 when Reliance Jio entered the market with disruptive pricing. Aircel was forced to slash tariffs, profits vanished, and debt piled up to nearly ₹50,000 crore.

In February 2018, Aircel officially went bankrupt.

Yet the story doesn't end there. Despite losing Aircel, founder C. Sivasankaran remains a successful entrepreneur and is now active in the health and wellness sector.

snippet.title: Shocking Valuation Downfall Story of Cred | Startup Case Study
snippet.description:
Why is Cred’s valuation collapsing from 6.4 billion dollars in 2022 to just 3.5 billion dollars in 2025? Startup Valuation Downfall Case Study in Telugu | fintech startup case study | venture capital India | startup valuation analysis | unit economics case study

Instant IT Expert Help: https://planbnext.com/

In June 2022, CRED reached its peak valuation of $6.4 billion after raising $140 million in a Series F round led by Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund, GIC. This round, which also included Tiger Global and Sofina, was priced at an exceptionally aggressive premium, trading at a massive ~136x multiple on its trailing FY22 revenue. This valuation reflected the peak of the private market boom, pricing the company far beyond standard public market metrics.

However, in 2025, the company executed a "strategic reset" through a downround to clean up its capitalization table. CRED raised approximately $75 million—once again led by GIC—but at a sharply corrected valuation of $3.5 billion. This represents a 45% haircut from its 2022 peak. The markdown was a deliberate move to unwind the inflated 2022 premium and align the company with realistic revenue multiples (closer to 5x-10x) in preparation for a future IPO.
Would you like me to write a script for your YouTube channel analyzing this specific price correction?

09:25 Comparison with other Startups

Cred was once celebrated as one of India’s hottest fintech startups. In 2022, investors valued Cred at 6.4 billion dollars. By 2025, that valuation dropped to around 3.5 billion dollars. At the same time, its entire business model started facing heavy pressure from RBI regulations, slowing revenue growth, and increasing doubts about long-term stability.

The core idea behind Cred, according to founder Kunal Shah, was to gather India’s most creditworthy users — people with 750+ credit scores who pay their credit card bills on time — into one premium platform and later sell them high-quality financial products.  The initial hook was simple: a smooth, premium-looking app that let you pay all credit card bills in one place, supported by celebrity IPL ads and attractive rewards. But once those rewards were reduced, many early users felt disappointed.

Slowly, Cred began adding products on top of its user base. Cred RentPay let users pay house rent via credit card and earn points while Cred charged a fee. It worked for a while, but banks removed rewards and added extra charges. Then RBI introduced stricter norms allowing credit card payments only to genuine businesses, which effectively killed most individual rent transactions. One major revenue vertical disappeared.

Lending then became Cred’s real engine. Through Cred Stash (later Cred Cash), users could take instant loans up to a few lakhs at 12–30% interest. The money came from partner banks and NBFCs, while Cred earned 10–15% of the interest. Soon, 80–90% of Cred’s revenue came from this lending model. But after RBI increased risk weights on unsecured loans, banks had to lock more capital, raised interest rates, and tightened lending. Loans became costlier, and Cred’s revenue growth slowed.

To improve margins, Cred backed its own NBFC, Newtap Finance, where Kunal Shah holds the majority and Cred holds a minority. The idea was cheaper bulk borrowing and higher-rate lending to Cred users. But RBI blocked Cred from fully owning the NBFC, limiting scale. Other experiments like Cred Mint (9% deposits), Cred Flash (BNPL), Cred Garage and more also faced regulatory issues. Today, Cred mainly functions like an instant loan app for a narrow high-credit-score segment.

Financially, growth has cooled. Revenue rose from ₹1,400 crores (FY23) to ₹2,473 crores (FY24)—a 66% jump. But for FY25, despite eight months passing, Cred hasn’t filed results. Estimates suggest around ₹3,000 crores, only 21% growth. With higher lending costs and RBI pressure, losses remain large and rising. Delayed results typically indicate weak numbers.

On valuation, Cred has raised nearly $1 billion, reaching a $3.5B valuation, partly supported by Kunal Shah’s own VC fund investing back in 2025. When compared to BharatPe, Groww, and Physics Wallah—all with similar or lower funding but comparable valuations and stronger unit economics—Cred’s performance is clearly weaker.

If you are serious about startups, fintech, and entrepreneurship, this is an important case study to understand how narrative and valuation can be very different from real financial performance. snippet.title: Tracking Suspected Members of the Pakistani Taliban | Taliban Hunters (full documentary) | FRONTLINE
snippet.description:
Inside a counterterrorism police unit in Karachi, Pakistan, dedicated to tracking down suspected members of the Pakistani Taliban. (Aired 2015)

This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://bit.ly/47DFzCb

And support your local PBS station here: https://www.pbs.org/donate

In the nearly five years since the Taliban seized control of Afghanistan, there’s been a dramatic increase in attacks within neighboring Pakistan by the militant group Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan, commonly called the Pakistani Taliban or TTP. Pakistan has accused Taliban-controlled Afghanistan of harboring the group and enabling it to launch cross-border attacks, which the Afghan government denies — and in recent weeks, the fight between the two countries escalated into what Pakistan’s government called “open war.”

Against this volatile backdrop, FRONTLINE’s 2015 documentary “Taliban Hunters” offers relevant history on TTP and Pakistani security forces’ fight against it. This short documentary went inside a Karachi-based counterterrorism police unit dedicated to tracking down Taliban suspects. 

As the documentary reported, TTP first emerged in 2007 and used to have only a small, underground presence in Karachi, Pakistan’s largest city. But by the time the documentary aired, the group had been gaining ground in the city of over 20 million people, and carrying out suicide bombings and targeted assassinations there.

The film documented how the unit carried out raids to take suspected TTP members into custody. It also explored human rights groups’ allegations that Karachi authorities were abusing militants captured in the city’s fight against terrorism. Amid TTP’s current resurgence, “Taliban Hunters” is an illuminating snapshot of where the fight against them stood in one large city back in 2015, and how the group operated.

“Taliban Hunters” is directed and reported by Mobeen Azhar and produced by Jamie Doran. The senior producer for FRONTLINE is Dan Edge.
